content_html:
PyNN

PyNN unifies spiking neural modeling across platforms. It abstracts simulator-specific code into a portable Python interface. For neuromorphic systems like SpiNNaker, PyNN serves as both a modeling language and a deployment framework, translating neural architectures into distributed, event-driven hardware processes.

PyNN is one of the most important software layers connecting biological neuroscience and neuromorphic hardware such as SpiNNaker, BrainScaleS, and Loihi. PyNN stands for Python Neural Networks (or Python for Neuronal Networks). It is an open-source Python API designed to provide a common programming interface for building, simulating, and analyzing models of spiking neural networks (SNNs) across different back-ends - whether they are software simulators or specialized neuromorphic chips.

PyNN lets you write one piece of code to describe a spiking neural network, and then run it on many kinds of hardware - without rewriting your model. It’s the bridge between neuroscience models and the various simulation or hardware platforms that implement them.

Before PyNN, researchers faced fragmentation:

  • Each simulator (e.g. NEURON, NEST, Brian) had its own syntax, configuration format, and units.
  • Porting a model between systems was tedious and error-prone.
  • Hardware like SpiNNaker or BrainScaleS needed completely different code.

PyNN standardizes this. It defines an abstraction layer for neuron types, synapses, connectivity patterns, and recording mechanisms. Your model becomes platform-agnostic - you can “plug in” different back-ends.

Core Abstractions

Concept Description Example
Population A group of neurons with the same model parameters pop = sim.Population(100, sim.IF_cond_exp())
Projection Connections between populations sim.Projection(pop1, pop2, connector, synapse_type)
Connector Defines connectivity (one-to-one, all-to-all, distance-dependent, etc.) sim.AllToAllConnector()
Synapse Dynamics Rules for plasticity (e.g. STDP) sim.STDPMechanism(timing_dependence=..., weight_dependence=...)
Recorders Specify what to measure (spikes, voltages, synaptic weights) pop.record(['spikes', 'v'])

Once defined, the same script can be executed on any PyNN-compatible simulator or hardware by simply changing one line:

import pyNN.nest as sim     # Run on NEST
# or
import pyNN.spiNNaker as sim  # Run on SpiNNaker
# or
import pyNN.brainscales as sim  # Run on BrainScaleS

Example

import pyNN.spiNNaker as sim

sim.setup(timestep=1.0)

pop1 = sim.Population(100, sim.IF_curr_exp(), label="Excitatory")
pop2 = sim.Population(100, sim.IF_curr_exp(), label="Inhibitory")

conn = sim.AllToAllConnector()
syn = sim.StaticSynapse(weight=0.05, delay=1.0)

sim.Projection(pop1, pop2, conn, syn)
pop1.record('spikes')

sim.run(1000)
data = pop1.get_data('spikes')
sim.end()

Back-Ends Supported

PyNN works with multiple targets, including:

Simulator / Hardware Type Notes
NEST Software simulator Large-scale, detailed neuron models
NEURON Software simulator Compartmental neuron models
Brian2 Software simulator Python-native, flexible
SpiNNaker Neuromorphic hardware Event-driven, real-time spiking
BrainScaleS Analog neuromorphic hardware Sub-millisecond accelerated simulation
Loihi Intel neuromorphic chip (via extensions) On-chip learning and low power

Thus, PyNN acts like a universal compiler for biological and neuromorphic modeling.

How PyNN Integrates with SpiNNaker

When used with SpiNNaker, PyNN scripts:

  • Define network structure and parameters in Python.
  • Are parsed by the SpiNNaker front-end software stack.
  • Translated into binary configuration data for individual SpiNNaker cores:
    • Each neuron population is mapped to a group of cores.
    • Synaptic weights and delays are programmed into memory.
    • Routing tables are built to represent network connections.
  • The SpiNNaker hardware then executes the network in real time.
  • Recorded spikes and data are sent back to the host PC for analysis.

So PyNN acts as both a modeling interface and a deployment toolchain.

Advantages

Advantage Explanation
Portability Run the same model on software or hardware back-ends.
Reproducibility Consistent syntax reduces variability between studies.
Interoperability Common ground for multi-lab collaboration.
Ease of learning Familiar Python environment.
Extensibility New neuron or synapse models can be added to any backend.

Think of PyNN as the “OpenGL” of neuroscience: OpenGL provides one interface for graphics across hardware, PyNN provides one interface for spiking neural simulations across back-ends. PyNN is the universal language for spiking neural networks. It abstracts away the differences between simulation engines and neuromorphic chips, enabling reproducible, cross-platform neuroscience and AI research.

For SpiNNaker, it serves as both:

  • a programming interface (to describe neural models), and
  • a deployment system (to map those models into distributed hardware processes).

It is the software layer that gives meaning to the spikes.
